passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel dietary supplement on the recovery of muscle strength after resistance training in healthy adults. Twenty-eight participants were randomly assigned to either the supplement group (n=14) or a placebo group (n=14). Over a 6‑week period, all subjects performed a standardized resistance‑training regimen three times per week. Muscle strength was assessed by measuring one‑repetition maximum (1RM) for the bench press and leg press at baseline, week 3, and week 6. In addition, serum creatine kinase (CK) levels were measured at the same time points to evaluate muscle damage. In the supplement group, bench‑press 1RM rose 12% from baseline to week 6 (Table 1), a gain significantly greater than that of the placebo group (p = 0.02). CK levels rose modestly in both groups but were significantly lower in the supplement group at week 6 (p = 0.04). These findings suggest that the supplement may enhance strength gains and reduce exercise‑induced muscle damage.
table_data:
Time Point | Bench 1RM (kg), supplement group | CK (U/L), supplement group | % Change in bench 1RM from baseline
Baseline | 100 ± 10 | 200 ± 30 | 0%
Week 3 | 110 ± 12 | 220 ± 35 | 10%
Week 6 | 112 ± 11 | 210 ± 32 | 12%
stem: Which of the following best describes the change in bench‑press 1RM for the supplement group from baseline to week 6?
explanation: Correct: Table 1 shows bench‑press 1RM rising from 100 to 112 kg in the supplement group, a 12% increase at week 6. Why the others are wrong: A) 10% is the week 3 value. C) 15% does not appear in the data. D) 8% does not appear in the data.
trap: Option A reflects the 10% increase reported at week 3, not week 6.

stem: What is the percent change in the supplement group's mean CK from baseline to week 6?
explanation: Correct: A) (210 - 200) / 200 x 100 = +5%, a small rise. Why the others are wrong: B) 4.8% divides the 10 U/L change by the week 6 value (210) instead of baseline. C) 10% is the week 3 percent change in bench 1RM, not CK. D) The sign is wrong; CK rose, it did not fall.
trap: Dividing the 10 U/L change by the week 6 value (210) gives 4.8% (B), and reading CK as falling (D) confuses it with the group comparison at week 6.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage and Table 1?

options.A: Bench‑press 1RM in the supplement group was higher at week 6 than at baseline.
options.B: At week 6, CK was significantly lower in the supplement group than in the placebo group.
options.C: In the supplement group, CK at week 6 was lower than at baseline.
options.D: Participants were randomly assigned to supplement or placebo.

explanation: Correct: Table 1 shows supplement group CK of 200 U/L at baseline and 210 U/L at week 6, a slight rise, not a fall. Why the others are wrong: A) 1RM rose from 100 to 112 kg. B) the passage reports lower CK in the supplement group at week 6 (p = 0.04). D) the passage states random assignment to groups of 14.
trap: Reading "lower than placebo" as "lower than its own baseline".

stem: Elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) after resistance exercise is a standard indicator of which process?

options.A: Leakage of muscle cell contents into the blood due to muscle fiber damage
options.B: Increased glucose uptake by adipose tissue
options.C: Reduced bile flow from the liver

explanation: Correct: CK is an intracellular muscle enzyme; when fibers are damaged it leaks into the blood, which is why the passage uses it to evaluate muscle damage. Why the others are wrong: B) adipose glucose uptake is not reflected by serum CK. C) reduced bile flow is assessed by liver markers such as bilirubin, not CK. D) thyroid hormone synthesis is assessed by TSH and thyroid hormones, not CK.
trap: Picking a metabolic or endocrine process because CK is "a blood enzyme", rather than recalling its muscle origin.
